query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Moderate-temperature thermal aging of non-equilibrium, Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys promotes diffusion‐driven phase separation that results in the precipitation and grain-boundary segregation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases. This microstructural evolution modifies the alloy’s surface chemistry such that, compared to the as‐cast state, the alloy develops a more protective, adherent oxide scale under high-temperature oxidation while altering its corrosion behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, non-equilibrium lightweight high-entropy alloy (density <6 g/cm³) with a metastable, relatively homogeneous mixture of a solid-solution matrix and dispersed precursor phases.
generation.intervention: A controlled, moderate-temperature isothermal annealing treatment performed below the melting point to induce diffusion-controlled phase separation.
generation.conditions: The alloy is aged under inert atmosphere conditions at a temperature that permits limited diffusion (e.g., several hundred °C) without reaching full equilibrium, followed by exposure to a corrosive aqueous environment at ambient temperature and separate high-temperature oxidation testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The precipitation and grain-boundary segregation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
generation.mechanism: During thermal aging, Mg atoms diffuse and segregate to form discrete Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates along grain boundaries and phase interfaces. These evolved microstructural features facilitate heterogeneous nucleation of a more continuous and adherent oxide layer under high-temperature conditions. Their influence on local electrochemical properties modifies the corrosion pathways compared to the homogeneous as-cast state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-cast baseline, thermally aged samples are expected to develop a more protective high-temperature oxide scale that enhances oxidation resistance. In addition, the redistributed Mg-rich phases will alter the corrosion behavior, with preliminary indications suggesting that overall corrosion performance may be improved although localized variations could arise.
generation.baseline: The as-cast alloy exhibiting a metastable, relatively uniform microstructure with minimal segregation of Mg and less-developed oxide scale characteristics.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis specifically applies to Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys (density <6 g/cm³) produced under non-equilibrium conditions; its relevance to alloys processed toward equilibrium or with significantly different compositions is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: While there is consensus on improved high-temperature oxidation resistance due to the evolved oxide scale, the net effect on corrosion resistance remains uncertain because similar thermal histories have been reported to both enhance overall protection and, in some cases, promote localized galvanic effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples from the same as-cast batch. Subject one set to a controlled moderate-temperature annealing treatment under an inert atmosphere while keeping the other set as the baseline. Perform detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM and XRD) to assess the formation and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. Subsequently, expose both sets to standardized corrosion tests (such as potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) and high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., thermogravimetric analysis and oxide scale cross-sectional imaging).
measurements: TEM and XRD for phase identification and grain-boundary segregation of Mg-rich intermetallics
Electrochemical measurements (potentiodynamic polarization, impedance spectroscopy) to assess corrosion behavior
High-temperature oxidation kinetics and oxide scale morphology (via TGA, SEM, and EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit significant precipitation and segregation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases, or if no statistically significant improvements in high-temperature oxidation resistance and modifications in corrosion behavior are observed (relative to the as-cast baseline), then the hypothesis would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In non‐equilibrium, Mg-containing lightweight high‐entropy alloys, metastable Mg-rich solid solutions and intermetallic compounds evolve through selective Mg segregation during high‐temperature oxidation. This segregation leads to the formation of discrete Mg‐rich oxide/hydroxide regions that promote a dual effect: improved overall high-temperature oxidation resistance via a coherent, passivating layer and increased localized galvanic corrosion due to phase contrast between oxidized and less-reactive matrix regions.
drafts.material_initial_state: An as-cast, non-equilibrium Mg-containing high-entropy alloy with a mix of metastable solid solutions and intermetallic compounds, designed for lightweight density (<6 g/cm3).
drafts.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled thermal oxidation (e.g., heating in an oxidizing atmosphere) and subsequent corrosive environment exposure.
drafts.conditions: Experiments performed at elevated temperatures sufficient to initiate Mg segregation (e.g., >300°C) under an oxygen-rich atmosphere, with corrosion tests conducted (e.g., salt spray or immersion tests) under identical sample histories. A controlled comparison is performed against an alloy sample maintained in the as-cast state.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of discrete Mg-rich oxide/hydroxide phases at internal boundaries and interfaces resulting from Mg segregation, which alters the microstructural continuity of the alloy.
drafts.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the metastable Mg-containing phases selectively oxidize, with Mg diffusing more rapidly and forming a continuous or semi-continuous MgO/Mg(OH)2 layer. This layer improves the overall oxidation resistance by acting as a barrier but, at the same time, creates localized electrochemical differences that serve as galvanic cells when the material is exposed to corrosive environments.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to its initial, non-equilibrium state, the thermally treated alloy should exhibit a more coherent oxide film that lowers oxidation rates at high temperatures, but concomitantly display increased susceptibility to localized corrosion due to arising micro-galvanic couples between the oxidized (Mg-rich) regions and the remaining unoxidized or less oxidized matrix.
drafts.baseline: As-cast non-equilibrium high-entropy alloy without any deliberate thermal oxidation, containing a uniform dispersion of metastable phases.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for lightweight high-entropy alloys (density <6 g/cm3) where Mg is a significant constituent alongside elements like Al, Cu, Zn, and Gd. It may not apply to alloys with different elemental compositions or alloys processed to achieve near-equilibrium microstructures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare specimens of the Mg-containing high-entropy alloy and subject one set to controlled high-temperature oxidation while keeping another set in the as-cast state. Characterize the microstructural evolution using SEM/TEM and compositional mapping to identify Mg-rich oxide/hydroxide formation. Then, perform standardized corrosion tests (e.g., salt spray exposure) on both sets.
measurements: High-resolution imaging (SEM/TEM) to detect and map Mg-rich oxide phases
Oxidation kinetics assessment (e.g., weight gain analysis)
Electrochemical corrosion measurements (e.g., corrosion current density and potential mapping)
Comparative analysis of phase distribution between thermally treated and as-cast samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally oxidized samples do not show significant formation of discrete Mg-rich oxide/hydroxide phases or if there is no measurable difference in either high-temperature oxidation resistance or localized corrosion (relative to the as-cast state), then the hypothesized mechanism (linking selective Mg segregation to dual functional property changes) would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Non‐equilibrium processing of Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys induces metastable microstructures with local Mg segregation that, upon controlled thermal aging, transform into protective intermetallic and Mg-enriched boundary phases. These phases, acting as oxidation and corrosion inhibitors, enhance the material’s performance relative to its initial homogeneous state.
drafts.material_initial_state: An induction‐melted MgAlCuZnGd alloy with a homogeneous metastable solid solution containing minor, dispersed intermetallic compounds, and density below 6 g/cm³.
drafts.intervention: Subject a set of as-cast alloys to a controlled thermal aging (annealing) treatment expected to promote the evolution of segregated phases.
drafts.conditions: Thermal treatment under aging temperatures (e.g., between 300°C and 500°C) below the melting point, keeping composition and density constraints constant; comparison made with a controlled, as-cast baseline sample.
drafts.structural_mediator: Protective intermetallic compounds and Mg-enriched grain boundary phases that nucleate during aging.
drafts.mechanism: During non-equilibrium solidification, Mg segregation occurs, creating compositional gradients. When thermally aged, these gradients promote the nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds and Mg-rich boundary phases which preferentially form protective oxide layers, reducing corrosion and high-temperature oxidation rates.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Aged samples will demonstrate lower corrosion rates and improved high-temperature oxidation behavior (e.g., more adherent, protective oxide scales) compared to the as-cast baseline.
drafts.baseline: The as-cast metastable MgAlCuZnGd alloy without intentional thermal aging, exhibiting a homogeneous solid solution and less-defined protective phase networks.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies only to non-equilibrium processed, Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys under the specified thermal aging conditions; its applicability to equilibrium-processed or significantly different compositional variants is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MgAlCuZnGd alloy samples via induction melting to ensure non-equilibrium microstructures. Subject one set to a controlled thermal aging treatment (e.g., 300°C–500°C for an appropriate duration) while keeping the other set in the as-cast state. Perform microstructural analysis (SEM, TEM, and XRD) to detect the formation of intermetallic compounds and Mg-enriched grain boundary phases. Subsequently, conduct standardized corrosion tests (such as potentiodynamic polarization) and high-temperature oxidation tests to compare the performance between the aged and as-cast samples.
measurements: Phase identification and distribution using microscopic and diffraction techniques
Corrosion rate (current density or weight loss measurements)
Oxidation behavior (oxide scale thickness, adherence, and weight gain measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not exhibit the predicted formation of protective phases (or if such phases are not significantly different from those in the as-cast baseline) and show no measurable improvement in corrosion resistance or high-temperature oxidation behavior, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, the primary evolution pathway is driven by the gradual precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases that segregate to grain boundaries and surfaces during post-solidification thermal exposure. This microstructural evolution simultaneously depletes Mg from the bulk and enriches the interface regions, thereby accelerating localized corrosion at ambient conditions while promoting the formation of a more protective Mg-rich oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation.
drafts.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium, as-cast lightweight high-entropy alloy with a nominally homogeneous mixture of solid-solution and intermetallic constituents but with metastable phase distributions.
drafts.intervention: Controlled thermal treatment (annealing) at elevated temperatures below the alloy's melting point to simulate prolonged service or processing conditions that drive phase separation.
drafts.conditions: Alloys maintained below 6 g/cm3 undergoing annealing in an inert atmosphere for controlled times to avoid complete equilibrium, with subsequent exposure to corrosive aqueous environments at room temperature and oxidative conditions at high temperature.
drafts.structural_mediator: The precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic phases and their segregation to grain boundaries and surfaces.
drafts.mechanism: Thermal exposure induces further phase separation in the non-equilibrium alloy, leading to the localized enrichment of Mg in interfacial regions. This change modifies the local electrochemical potential (enhancing corrosion susceptibility via galvanic effects) and, under high-temperature oxidation conditions, facilitates the formation of a dense, protective Mg-rich oxide scale that retards oxidation kinetics.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, annealed samples will show (1) increased localized corrosion rates due to the formation of galvanic sites at precipitate–matrix interfaces and (2) improved high-temperature oxidation resistance owing to the development of a more protective, continuous Mg-rich oxide scale.
drafts.baseline: As-cast alloy with metastable, relatively homogeneous phase distribution and less defined grain boundary segregation.
drafts.boundary: Applies to Mg-containing lightweight HEAs designed below 6 g/cm3 and prepared under non-equilibrium casting conditions, with thermal treatments that do not fully equilibrate the microstructure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sets of as-cast Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy samples and subject them to controlled annealing under identical thermal conditions. Characterize the evolution of the microstructure using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to identify the formation and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic phases. Perform potentiodynamic polarization tests and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to evaluate corrosion behavior at ambient room temperature. Additionally, conduct thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) during high-temperature oxidation to assess oxide scale development. Compare the property changes of annealed samples to the as-cast baseline.
measurements: Phase identification and grain boundary segregation via TEM and XRD
Corrosion rates using potentiodynamic polarization and EIS
Oxidation kinetics and scale quality using TGA and SEM/EDS analyses of scale cross-sections
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit significant precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallics and associated grain-boundary segregation, or if there is no observable increase in localized corrosion rates and enhanced high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast baseline, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In the as‐cast (non-equilibrium) Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy, moderate-temperature aging induces diffusion‐controlled phase separation that forms Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. These precipitates act as structural mediators that promote the development of an adherent, protective oxide scale during high-temperature exposure and inhibit localized corrosion, thereby enhancing the alloy’s overall high-temperature oxidation and corrosion resistance compared to the original as‐cast state.
drafts.material_initial_state: As‐cast Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy (Al–Mg–Cu–Zn–Gd or similar) exhibiting a metastable microstructure consisting of a dominant solid solution with some dispersed precursor phases.
drafts.intervention: A controlled moderate-temperature aging treatment (isothermal annealing) applied post-casting.
drafts.conditions: The aging is carried out under conditions that permit limited diffusion (e.g., 300–400°C for a defined period) without exceeding the density constraint (<6 g/cm³) or causing excessive grain growth.
drafts.structural_mediator: The precipitation of discrete Mg-rich intermetallic phases, especially along grain boundaries or phase interfaces.
drafts.mechanism: Aging enables diffusion-driven phase separation wherein Mg segregates to form intermetallic precipitates. These precipitates facilitate the heterogeneous nucleation and growth of a protective oxide layer during subsequent high-temperature exposure, and their presence also disrupts electrochemical pathways that would otherwise lead to rapid corrosion in the as-cast microstructure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the aged alloy should display a measurable reduction in corrosion rate (via electrochemical tests) and improved high-temperature oxidation performance (evidenced by a thicker, more continuous and adherent oxide scale).
drafts.baseline: As-cast alloy featuring a mixed-phase metastable structure without well-developed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates or a mature protective oxide scale.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with overall densities below 6 g/cm³ and similar compositional ranges (e.g., containing Al, Mg, Cu, Zn, Gd) where both solid solution and intermetallic phases are present.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set maintained in the as-cast state and the other subjected to a controlled moderate-temperature aging treatment. Perform detailed microstructural analyses (XRD, SEM-EDS) to identify the formation of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. Then, subject both sets to corrosion tests (e.g., electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, potentiodynamic polarization) and high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., thermogravimetric analysis to monitor weight gain and oxide scale morphology analysis).
measurements: SEM-EDS to map the distribution and composition of precipitates
Electrochemical corrosion measurements (e.g., corrosion rate, impedance)
High-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., weight gain and oxide layer characterization)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aging treatment does not lead to the formation of detectable Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, or if the aged samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior (as compared to as-cast samples), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
